consumer_seed: The Ofcom unable-to-pay guide was published on 13 March 2013.
The Ofcom unable-to-pay guide was last updated on 8 April 2026.
Ofcom advises customers having difficulty paying a bill not to ignore it.
A customer having payment difficulty should contact the phone provider as soon as possible.
A customer can ask the provider about moving to a cheaper package.
A customer can ask whether debt can be paid over time.
A customer can ask whether monthly payments can be reduced to an affordable rate.
A customer can ask whether part of the debt may be waived if the remainder is paid within an agreed time.
A customer can ask about changing the payment date or switching to direct debit.
Ofcom lists selling old mobile handsets for recycling as a possible way to raise funds.
A customer can ask the provider for details of debt-advice agencies.
Providers are not obliged to offer every listed payment-support option.
The Ofcom billing-and-charges complaint guide was published on 19 July 2023.
The Ofcom billing-and-charges complaint guide was last updated on 8 April 2026.
Ofcom does not handle individual billing complaints through the guide.
The first step for an individual billing problem is to contact the provider's customer-services department.
If customer service does not resolve the issue, the customer should make a formal complaint to the provider.
Formal-complaint details may be found on the bill, provider website or from customer services.
An unresolved complaint can be escalated by asking the provider for a deadlock letter.
After six weeks from the first formal complaint, the customer can contact the relevant ADR scheme directly.
The Ofcom stopping-premium-rate-charges guide was published on 31 January 2025.
The guide was last updated on 23 June 2025.
For an unexpected phone-bill charge, the customer should first contact the service provider responsible for the service.
A phone-paid purchase can involve both a premium-rate-service provider and the mobile or fixed-line network.
The premium-rate-service provider supplies the service or content being purchased.
The network adds the charge to the bill or deducts it from credit on behalf of the service provider.
The mobile network is not normally responsible for managing the premium-rate service itself.
A mobile network can help identify the service provider when the customer does not know who charged them.
The phone bill is the primary place to check whether a premium-rate-service charge was applied.
A phone bill may list a number rather than the premium-rate-service provider's name.
Mobile text short codes are commonly five or six digits and may start with 5, 6, 7 or 8.
Charge-to-mobile, Operator Billing, Direct Carrier Billing and Google Play can describe payment mechanisms rather than provider names.
Directory-enquiry 118 numbers and 09, 087 and some 084 numbers can be premium-rate services.
Ofcom rules require that customers are not charged for a premium-rate service without consent.
Ofcom rules require the cost and operation of a premium-rate service to be clear.
The service provider should be able to explain the charge, the service used and when it was used.
A customer can text STOP ALL to the number supplied by the service provider to stop recurring charges.
A customer seeking a refund should first request it from the premium-rate-service provider.
A premium-rate-service complaint should be resolved quickly and easily under the applicable rules.
Ofcom uses reports for enforcement and policy work but does not resolve individual premium-rate-service complaints.
The Ofcom abuse, harassment and violence telecoms guide was published on 28 May 2025.
The guide advises considering telecoms security, accessibility and costs when abuse, harassment or violence is involved.
Controlling another person's phone use or impersonating them through a mobile can be coercive control.
Ofcom states that coercive control is a criminal offence and should be reported to the police.
A person forced into an unsuitable contract or debt can ask the provider to close the account or cancel the contract.
A provider is not obliged in every case to close an account or cancel a contract requested because of abuse.
A customer can ask a provider to change the correspondence address or phone number to improve safety.
Ofcom expects providers to treat victims of harassment or abuse fairly and sympathetically.
Unwanted callers or texters can usually be blocked from the recent-calls list or messaging application.
Blocking withheld numbers can also block legitimate calls, so the guide notes a trade-off.
Do-not-disturb settings can reduce unwanted contact while allowing other safety choices.
The guide advises logging out of accounts and reviewing devices or apps that share location information.
Communications providers should generally take instructions only from the named account holder unless an authorised arrangement applies.
A person on a family mobile plan controlled by an abuser can contact the provider for advice on available options.
A telecoms account held in another person's name cannot normally be transferred without that account holder's permission.
The account holder may be able to see called numbers through itemised billing.
A person who left a property because of violence can ask the broadband or landline provider to close the account without penalty.
Calls to 0800 numbers are free and do not appear on itemised bills.
For temporary accommodation, the guide notes mobile data, tethering and 4G or 5G routers as possible alternatives to a long fixed-broadband contract.
